source.title: Building from the ground up: augmentation strategies to improve protein language model performance on protein sets
source.authors: Emily M. Stump; H. Dennison; P. Strobbia; G-Bv Stan; R. Dima

record.file_problem: none noted; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream performance across differently sized protein language models in a protein contact-prediction task, a new domain and task relative to the cited language-model scaling work. It does not measure pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports downstream MCC for contact-map prediction across three pretrained protein language models with different parameter counts. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy, sweep training tokens or compute, fit power laws, or test compute-optimal allocations. Results about data ablation and synthetic augmentation do not directly measure the claim versions beyond their implications for downstream performance.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. It compares three pLMs from different families (ESM-2 8M, AminoBERT 87M, ProtBERT 420M), which differ in architecture, pretraining corpus and pretraining setup, on one fine-tuned downstream task. There is no within-family size sweep, even though ESM-2 sizes from 8M to 15B were available and only 8M was used. The study reports no pretraining loss. ProtBERT's poor result is a failure to fit: train MCC struggles to pass 0.2. The authors attribute this to too little fine-tuning data, not to pretraining scale. So the comparison cannot show whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6). The study cites Kaplan et al. only to motivate data hunger. Its aim is dataset ablation and active-learning augmentation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors conclude that with limited data, narrowing the dataset's scope (targeted ablation) keeps in-distribution performance high but overfits and generalises worse to the full test distribution. Uniform ablation degrades performance as size shrinks. ESM-3-generated augmentation via disagreement-based active learning helps modestly, mainly on targeted sets above a minimum size, and hurts on very small sets. On model size, they say only that ProtBERT (420M) underperformed ∼0.5-MCC smaller models, reaching ∼0.3, likely because DIPS-Plus is too small for it.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains pretrained protein-language-model encoders for a downstream contact-map task and measures MCC. It does not reproduce the original text-pretraining loss, model/token/compute sweeps, or compute-optimal fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream MCC changes with dataset size and scope: uniform ablations generally benefit from more data, while targeted ablations can improve in-distribution results but perform worse on the unablated test distribution. Model size also interacts with available training data.

fits_no_version.finding: On full DIPS-Plus contact-map prediction, the largest pLM tested (ProtBERT, 420M) reached lower MCC (∼0.2–0.3) than ESM-2 8M and AminoBERT 87M (∼0.5). The authors attribute this to fine-tuning data being too small for a model of that size. The models differ in family, pretraining data and architecture.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger pretrained encoders can underperform smaller ones on a downstream task when the fine-tuning dataset is too small (fine-tuning data sufficiency vs. model size).

record.problems: Only one dataset and one downstream task are used, with three non-identical model architectures and pretraining setups rather than a controlled scale sweep. MCC values cited in the text are approximate; numerical uncertainty values are not given there.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss and no sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
All; only the downstream MLP head's depth and width were hyperparameter-tuned.
All; no power-law fits in protein models or fine-tuning.
All: no controlled scale sweep and no pretraining-loss relationship; only three confounded cross-family models.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' with a V6 'challenges' label is overturned. The three pLMs are not a scale series: different families, pretraining corpora and architectures, and per-model hyperparameter optimisation of a downstream head. ProtBERT's low train MCC indicates a training failure rather than a scale effect. The text gives inconsistent ProtBERT values: <0.2 even on train in the Results, ∼0.3 in the Conclusions.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law form and range.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power-law fits on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds in protein models or fine-tuning; no loss-law fits are reported.
No pretraining-loss relationship or controlled scale sweep; only three distinct protein language models are compared on one downstream task.

rows.check: 'Reversed' is not supportable. ProtBERT differs from the others in architecture and pretraining, not only in size, and it largely failed to train: Results say MCC 'struggle[s] to surpass 0.2 even on the training set'. That conflicts with the ∼0.3 in the Conclusions; the value should note both. This is a fine-tuning or data-sufficiency observation, not pretraining-scale evidence.
